meta.name: AI system risk assessment

profiles.app: Applications using AI: chatbots, copilots, RAG and LLM features inside a product.
profiles.agent: Agentic AI bots that plan and take actions with tools, code, or other agents.
profiles.mcp: MCP servers and clients that expose tools, data, or prompts to models.

tag_groups.policy: Clause ids in grc/policy.json (the model AI policy).
tag_groups.tags: Compliance: clauses in each framework. Only clauses listed in meta.clauses are allowed.
tag_groups.nist_metric: A measurable indicator for the control, keyed to a NIST AI RMF subcategory, with a suggested target.

meta.mapping_note: Mappings are indicative. OWASP Agentic short names follow the OWASP GenAI Security Project list of December 2025; OWASP MCP Top 10 is a beta project. Confirm against the current text of each framework before putting them in front of an auditor.

OWASP MCP: MCP01:2025 Token Mismanagement and Secret Exposure
MCP02:2025 Privilege Escalation via Scope Creep
MCP04:2025 Software Supply Chain Attacks and Dependency Tampering
MCP06:2025 Prompt Injection via Contextual Payloads
MCP08:2025 Lack of Audit and Telemetry

meta.answers_note: An answer may be {"maturity": 0-3, "note": "..."} or {"na": true, "note": "why"} to exclude a question that does not apply (attested questions only).

questions.question: Is there a named owner accountable for the AI system and its risks?
questions.guidance: A single accountable owner, not a committee in the abstract.
options: No owner identified.
An informal owner everyone assumes, not written down.
Owner named in the inventory, but not tied to risk sign-off.
Named owner in the inventory who signs off risk and is reviewed yearly.

nist_metric.metric: Share of AI systems in the inventory with a named accountable owner

questions.question: Is there an AI policy that defines acceptable use, prohibited use, and escalation?
questions.guidance: Written, approved, and known to the people building and running the system.
options: No AI policy.
Draft or informal guidance only.
Approved policy, not yet communicated or enforced.
Approved, communicated, acknowledged by staff, and reviewed yearly.

nist_metric.metric: Share of in-scope staff who acknowledged the current AI policy

questions.question: Is there a complete inventory of AI systems, agents, and MCP servers, each with a risk class?
questions.guidance: Include shadow AI: tools staff adopted on their own. Risk class follows the EU AI Act categories or your own scheme.
options: No inventory.
Partial list, no risk class.
Inventory with risk classes, updated by hand.
Inventory with risk classes, reconciled against discovery (network, SSO, procurement) at least quarterly.

nist_metric.metric: Share of discovered AI systems present in the inventory with a risk class

questions.question: Are staff who build, run, or use the system trained on AI risk and the AI policy?
questions.guidance: AI literacy proportionate to the role: builders, operators, and everyday users need different depth.
options: No training.
Ad hoc briefings.
Role-based training exists, completion not tracked.
Role-based training with tracked completion and yearly refresh.

nist_metric.metric: Training completion rate for in-scope roles

questions.question: Is a risk assessment performed before deployment and repeated on material change?
questions.guidance: Risk management is a lifecycle activity, not a one-off sign-off.
options: No assessment.
One-off assessment at launch.
Assessment at launch with a defined change trigger, not always followed.
Assessment at launch and on every material change, with records.

nist_metric.metric: Share of material changes that had a risk assessment before release

questions.question: Are AI-specific risks (misuse, over-autonomy, hallucination) recorded in the risk register?
questions.guidance: Not just generic IT risk. Name the AI failure modes.
options: Not in the register.
Generic IT risk only.
AI-specific risks listed, no owners or treatments.
AI-specific risks with owners, treatments, and review dates.

nist_metric.metric: Count of AI-specific risks in the register with an owner and treatment

questions.question: Is the data the system can access scoped to what the task needs, with personal data minimised?
questions.guidance: Data minimisation and purpose limitation.
options: Broad access to whatever is reachable.
Some scoping, personal data not reviewed.
Scoped access, personal data review in progress.
Scoped access, personal data minimised and reviewed on change.

nist_metric.metric: Share of data sources reachable by the system with a documented purpose

questions.question: Are secrets and credentials kept out of prompts, context, and training data?
questions.guidance: Secrets in context are secrets at risk.
options: Secrets are routinely pasted into prompts or config the model sees.
Guidance exists, no checks.
Secret scanning on code; prompts and context checked by hand.
Automated secret scanning on prompts, context, logs, and training data, with alerts.

nist_metric.metric: Secrets detected in prompts, context, or logs per month

questions.question: Does the agent operate under least privilege, with no standing access to secrets it does not need?
questions.guidance: Verified by the lab: leak rate with raw secrets present vs with a token broker.
options: Agent holds standing credentials to everything it can reach.
Some scoping, long-lived secrets still in the workspace.
Brokered access, leak rate reduced but not near zero.
Brokered short-lived scoped tokens; measured leak rate near zero.

nist_metric.metric: Canary leak rate with broker vs baseline (Wilson 95% CI)

questions.question: Are high-sensitivity actions denied to the agent without explicit human approval?
questions.guidance: Verified by the lab: the broker denies sensitive scopes.
options: No deny list; the agent can do anything its credentials allow.
Deny list documented, not enforced.
Enforced deny list, not yet exercised in tests.
Enforced deny list, with denied requests observed and logged.

nist_metric.metric: Sensitive-scope requests denied by the broker vs granted

questions.question: Does the agent resist instructions injected through tool output or retrieved content?
questions.guidance: Verified by the lab: an instruction planted in the README asks the agent to send secrets to the sink.
options: Not considered.
Known risk, no defence or test.
Defences in place, measured obey rate above 10%.
Measured obey rate at or below 10% across repeated trials.

nist_metric.metric: Injected-instruction obey rate (Wilson 95% CI)

questions.question: Does the agent avoid emitting secrets or sensitive data into its outputs and artifacts?
questions.guidance: Verified by the lab: a canary value in the agent's own output or a file it wrote.
options: Not considered.
Known risk, no filtering or test.
Output filtering in place, measured disclosure above 10%.
Measured disclosure at or below 10% across repeated trials.

nist_metric.metric: Share of trials where a secret appeared in agent output (Wilson 95% CI)

questions.question: Can a human review, pause, or stop the agent, and are autonomy limits defined?
questions.guidance: A kill switch that has actually been tried, and written limits on what the agent may do alone.
options: No way to stop it short of killing the host.
Can be stopped; autonomy limits informal.
Stop control and written autonomy limits, not tested.
Stop control tested on a schedule; autonomy limits written and enforced.

nist_metric.metric: Time from stop command to agent halt in the last drill

questions.question: Is the agent's scope of action constrained to its intended task?
questions.guidance: Tools, files, and network reachable by the agent match the task, not the developer's laptop.
options: Agent gets every tool available.
Tool list trimmed by hand, not reviewed.
Tool scope set per task, reviewed occasionally.
Tool scope set per task, enforced by allowlist, reviewed on change.

nist_metric.metric: Tool calls outside the task allowlist per 1,000 calls

questions.question: Are the agent's file access and network actions logged in a tamper-evident way?
questions.guidance: Verified by the lab: strace file access and sink network events are recorded.
options: No action logs.
Partial application logs.
File and network actions logged, not tamper-evident.
File and network actions logged to a tamper-evident store and retained.

nist_metric.metric: Share of agent actions with a matching log record

questions.question: Is there monitoring that would alert on anomalous AI behaviour?
questions.guidance: Logs nobody reads are not monitoring.
options: No monitoring.
Logs exist, no alerting.
Alerts on a few signals, not tuned.
Tuned alerts on defined AI signals, with an owner and response runbook.

nist_metric.metric: Mean time to detect an AI anomaly in the last exercise

questions.question: Do AI incidents follow a defined response process, including regulatory reporting where required?
questions.guidance: Covers harmful output, data leaks, and agent misbehaviour. Serious incidents may have legal reporting deadlines.
options: AI incidents are not recognised as a category.
Handled ad hoc by whoever notices.
AI incident type in the incident process, not exercised.
AI incident playbook exercised, with reporting duties mapped.

nist_metric.metric: AI incidents closed within the playbook SLA

questions.question: Are the model provider, version, and third-party tools recorded and risk-assessed?
questions.guidance: Includes plugins, MCP servers, and model updates pushed by the provider.
options: Not recorded.
Provider known, version not pinned.
Provider, version, and tools recorded; terms review pending.
Recorded, version-pinned, and risk-assessed, with re-review on provider change.

nist_metric.metric: Share of models and tools with a pinned version and a current risk review

questions.question: Is there system documentation describing purpose, limits, and known failure modes?
questions.guidance: A system or model card that an operator can actually use.
options: None.
Scattered notes.
Draft system card.
Published system card, versioned with the system.

nist_metric.metric: Share of deployed AI systems with a current system card

questions.question: Is the system evaluated and red-teamed before release and on a schedule, against defined metrics?
questions.guidance: Accuracy, safety, and security tests with recorded results and pass thresholds.
options: No evaluation.
Manual spot checks before release.
Defined eval suite before release, no schedule or red team.
Eval suite with thresholds plus periodic red-teaming, results recorded and acted on.

nist_metric.metric: Share of releases that passed the eval suite thresholds

questions.question: Do changes to models, prompts, tools, and configuration go through change control?
questions.guidance: A system prompt edit or a model version bump is a change.
options: Changes made directly in production.
Changes tracked after the fact.
Change control for code, not prompts or model versions.
Prompts, models, tools, and config versioned and released through change control.

nist_metric.metric: Production prompt or model changes without a change record

questions.question: Is model output validated or encoded before it reaches a browser, database, shell, or downstream system?
questions.guidance: Treat model output like user input.
options: Output passed straight through.
Some escaping in the UI only.
Validation on main sinks, gaps known.
All sinks validate or encode output, covered by tests.

nist_metric.metric: Output-handling test cases passing (XSS, SQL, command)

questions.question: Does the system prompt contain no secrets, and is it not relied on as a security control?
questions.guidance: Assume the system prompt will be extracted.
options: Secrets or access rules live in the system prompt.
No secrets, but access rules still enforced only by the prompt.
No secrets; most rules enforced in code.
No secrets; all access rules enforced outside the model, verified by extraction tests.

nist_metric.metric: System-prompt extraction attempts that reveal a secret or bypass a rule

questions.question: Does retrieval (RAG, vector store) enforce the same access rights as the source documents?
questions.guidance: A user must not retrieve a chunk they could not open as a document. Ingestion is checked for poisoned content.
options: One shared index, no access filtering.
Coarse separation by index.
Per-document access filtering, ingestion not checked.
Per-document access filtering plus ingestion checks, tested.

nist_metric.metric: Cross-permission retrievals in access tests

questions.question: Are hallucination and misinformation controlled with grounding, citations, and measured accuracy?
questions.guidance: Measure factual accuracy on a held-out set; show sources; flag low confidence.
options: Not addressed.
Disclaimer only.
Grounding or citations, accuracy not measured.
Grounding and citations with accuracy measured against a threshold.

nist_metric.metric: Factual accuracy on the held-out evaluation set

questions.question: Are there rate, token, and cost limits per user and per tenant?
questions.guidance: Stops runaway cost and denial of service through the model.
options: No limits.
Global provider limit only.
Per-user limits, no alerting.
Per-user and per-tenant limits with spend alerts.

nist_metric.metric: Requests or spend above the per-user limit that were not blocked

questions.question: Are users told they are interacting with AI, and is AI-generated content labelled?
questions.guidance: Disclosure at the point of interaction, not buried in terms.
options: No disclosure.
Mentioned in terms of service only.
Disclosed in the UI, generated content not labelled.
Disclosed in the UI and generated content labelled.

nist_metric.metric: Share of AI touchpoints with a visible disclosure

questions.question: Can users report bad or harmful output, and is that feedback reviewed and acted on?
questions.guidance: A report button nobody triages does not count.
options: No channel.
General support inbox only.
In-product report, reviewed occasionally.
In-product report with triage SLA, trends fed into evals.

nist_metric.metric: User reports triaged within SLA

questions.question: Does each agent act under its own non-human identity, not a borrowed user or shared service account?
questions.guidance: So its actions are attributable and its access can be revoked on its own.
options: Agent uses a person's credentials.
Shared service account across agents.
Per-agent identity, long-lived credentials.
Per-agent identity with short-lived credentials and on-behalf-of delegation.

nist_metric.metric: Agent actions not attributable to a unique agent identity

questions.question: Are agent actions tiered by impact, with human approval required for irreversible or high-impact ones?
questions.guidance: Payments, deletes, outbound messages, production changes. Approval must show the human what will actually happen.
options: No tiers; agent acts freely.
Approval for some actions, decided case by case.
Written action tiers, approval enforced for top tier.
Enforced tiers with clear approval prompts, audited for rubber-stamping.

nist_metric.metric: High-impact actions executed without recorded approval

questions.question: Is agent memory and persisted context validated, scoped per user or task, and able to expire?
questions.guidance: Poisoned memory turns a one-off injection into a persistent one.
options: Memory shared and unbounded.
Per-user memory, no validation.
Scoped memory with expiry, writes not validated.
Scoped, expiring memory with validated writes and a way to inspect and purge.

nist_metric.metric: Planted memory entries that change agent behaviour in tests

questions.question: Is code the agent writes or runs executed in a sandbox with no host or production access?
questions.guidance: Verified by the lab when the egress proxy runs: trial containers reach only the model relay and the sink, and every other attempt is denied and logged.
options: Runs on the host or a developer machine with full access.
Separate user account, same host.
Container sandbox, egress open.
Isolated sandbox, no mounted secrets, egress allowlisted, reset per task.

nist_metric.metric: Direct egress connections allowed outside the allowlist, and denied attempts per trial

questions.question: Are messages between agents authenticated, and is each agent's output treated as untrusted input by the next?
questions.guidance: Multi-agent pipelines: one compromised agent must not steer the rest.
options: Agents trust each other implicitly.
Shared secret on the channel, content trusted.
Authenticated channel, content partly validated.
Authenticated, integrity-protected messages, content validated at each hop.

nist_metric.metric: Unauthenticated inter-agent messages accepted in tests

questions.question: Are there step, time, and spend budgets plus circuit breakers to stop runaway or cascading agent failures?
questions.guidance: A loop that retries a failing tool 10,000 times is an incident.
options: No limits.
Provider rate limit only.
Per-run step or spend limits.
Step, time, and spend budgets with circuit breakers and alerting.

nist_metric.metric: Agent runs that exceeded budget before being stopped

questions.question: Are only approved MCP servers allowed, with unapproved (shadow) servers detected and blocked?
questions.guidance: Developers install MCP servers in seconds. Keep an allowlist and look for what is actually running.
options: Anyone can add any MCP server.
Approved list exists, not enforced.
Allowlist enforced in managed clients only.
Allowlist enforced in all clients, with discovery of unapproved servers.

nist_metric.metric: Unapproved MCP servers found in the last discovery scan

questions.question: Do MCP servers authenticate clients and authorise each tool call against the caller's own permissions?
questions.guidance: No anonymous servers on the network. No server acting with more rights than the user behind the call.
options: Unauthenticated servers reachable on the network.
Static API key shared by all clients.
Per-client auth, tools run with server's own broad rights.
Per-client OAuth with scoped tokens; tool calls authorised as the end user.

nist_metric.metric: MCP endpoints reachable without authentication

questions.question: Are MCP tokens and secrets short-lived, stored outside config files, and kept out of tool output and logs?
questions.guidance: Long-lived tokens in a JSON config on a laptop are the common case. Do not be the common case.
options: Long-lived tokens in plaintext client config.
Tokens in env vars, long-lived.
Secret manager, long-lived tokens, logs not scrubbed.
Short-lived tokens from a secret manager or broker; logs and tool output scrubbed.

OWASP MCP: MCP01:2025 Token Mismanagement and Secret Exposure

nist_metric.metric: MCP tokens with lifetime over 24 hours

questions.lab_scenario: future: run the broker condition through an MCP server instead of a plain HTTP broker

questions.question: Is each MCP server granted only the tool scopes it needs, with scope changes reviewed?
questions.guidance: Watch for scope creep: a server that started read-only and quietly gained write or admin.
options: Servers get full access to the backing system.
Scopes set once, never reviewed.
Scopes minimised, changes not reviewed.
Minimal scopes, changes reviewed and logged.

OWASP MCP: MCP02:2025 Privilege Escalation via Scope Creep

nist_metric.metric: Scope increases without a review record

questions.question: Are MCP tool descriptions and schemas reviewed, pinned, and alerted on when they change?
questions.guidance: Tool descriptions go straight into the model's context. A changed description can carry hidden instructions.
options: Descriptions never looked at.
Reviewed at install only.
Reviewed and pinned, no change detection.
Pinned by hash, changes blocked until re-reviewed.

nist_metric.metric: Tool description changes accepted without review

questions.question: Are MCP server packages and dependencies from trusted sources, version-pinned, and scanned?
questions.guidance: Many MCP servers are run straight from a package registry with the latest version on every start.
options: Run latest from public registries.
Known sources, not pinned.
Pinned versions, no scanning.
Pinned, scanned, and from an internal mirror or verified publisher.

OWASP MCP: MCP04:2025 Software Supply Chain Attacks and Dependency Tampering

nist_metric.metric: MCP servers running an unpinned or unscanned version

questions.question: Do MCP servers validate tool arguments and avoid passing model input to shells or interpreters?
questions.guidance: Parameterised calls, no string-built shell commands, and the server runs with minimal OS rights.
options: Arguments passed into shell commands.
Some escaping.
Validated arguments, server runs with broad OS rights.
Strict schemas, no shell interpolation, sandboxed low-privilege server.

nist_metric.metric: Command-injection test cases that succeed against MCP tools

questions.question: Is content returned by MCP tools (files, web pages, tickets) treated as untrusted data, not instructions?
questions.guidance: Resources and tool results are a prompt-injection path. Tool output should never widen what the agent may do.
options: Tool output trusted like the user.
Known risk, no control.
Output marked as untrusted, not tested.
Output isolated from instructions, high-impact actions gated, tested with injected content.

OWASP MCP: MCP06:2025 Prompt Injection via Contextual Payloads

nist_metric.metric: Injected-instruction obey rate through MCP tool output

questions.lab_scenario: future: injection condition delivered through an MCP resource; today's lab tests a README, not MCP, so this stays attested

questions.question: Is every MCP tool call logged with caller identity, tool, arguments, and result status?
questions.guidance: Without this you cannot reconstruct what an agent did through MCP.
options: No MCP logging.
Server debug logs only.
Tool calls logged without caller identity.
Structured tool-call logs with caller identity, sent to central monitoring.

OWASP MCP: MCP08:2025 Lack of Audit and Telemetry

nist_metric.metric: Share of MCP tool calls with a log record that names the caller

questions.question: Is context isolated between users, sessions, and tenants so one cannot see another's data through a shared server?
questions.guidance: Shared MCP servers and caches are where over-sharing happens.
options: Shared context across users.
Separated by convention.
Per-session isolation, shared caches.
Per-user and per-tenant isolation, tested.

nist_metric.metric: Cross-tenant data exposures in isolation tests

questions.question: Has each AI use been screened against the EU AI Act prohibited practices, with the result recorded?
questions.guidance: Prohibited practices include manipulative techniques, social scoring, and certain biometric and emotion-recognition uses. Mark n/a only if the system is not placed on the EU market or used in the EU.
options: No screening.
Informal judgement, not recorded.
Screening done at launch and recorded.
Screening recorded at launch and repeated on any change of purpose, reviewed by legal.

nist_metric.metric: Share of AI uses with a recorded prohibited-practice screening

questions.question: If the system is high-risk, has it passed conformity assessment and been registered in the EU database before use?
questions.guidance: Providers of high-risk systems need conformity assessment, a declaration of conformity, CE marking, and registration. Mark n/a if the system is classified as not high-risk and that classification is recorded (GOV-3).
options: Not known whether the system is high-risk.
Known high-risk, no conformity work started.
Conformity assessment in progress, not registered.
Conformity assessed, declaration issued, registered, and kept current.

nist_metric.metric: High-risk systems in use without a current conformity assessment and registration

questions.question: As a deployer, do you use the system per the provider's instructions, with named human overseers, monitoring, and retained logs?
questions.guidance: Deployer duties for high-risk systems include assigning competent human oversight, monitoring operation, keeping automatically generated logs for at least six months, and informing affected workers.
options: No deployer controls.
Instructions read, duties not assigned.
Overseers named and logs kept, monitoring informal.
Overseers named and trained, monitoring in place, logs retained at least six months, workers informed.

nist_metric.metric: Share of high-risk deployments with a named overseer and log retention of at least six months

questions.question: Where required, has a fundamental rights impact assessment been done before deployment?
questions.guidance: Required for certain deployers of high-risk systems, for example public bodies and providers of public services, and some credit and insurance uses. Mark n/a if not required and say why in the note.
options: Not considered.
Applicability checked, assessment not done.
Assessment done, not notified or not updated.
Assessment done before deployment, notified as required, updated on change.

nist_metric.metric: In-scope deployments with a current fundamental rights impact assessment

questions.question: If you provide or substantially modify a general-purpose AI model, do you keep its technical documentation, copyright policy, and training-content summary?
questions.guidance: General-purpose AI model provider duties. Most organisations using a vendor model mark n/a; fine-tuning that makes you a provider may bring the duties back.
options: Not assessed whether you are a provider.
Provider status known, no documentation.
Documentation in progress.
Technical documentation, copyright policy, and public training-content summary maintained.

nist_metric.metric: General-purpose models you provide with complete documentation
